an1.198:1.1: Cūḷapanthaka was slow of understanding, rejected even by his brother Mahāpanthaka, but then, supported by the Buddha, he achieved mastery ([thag10.4]()). He was praised at [ud5.10](), and gave effective instruction to the nuns at [pli-tv-bu-vb-pc22:1.1]().
an1.199:1.1: The obscure terms “turning away of the mind” (_cetovivaṭṭa_) and “turning away through perception” (_saññāvivaṭṭa_) are explained in the late canonical Paṭisambhidāmagga. One “turns away” the mind from “manifold” things such as sensual desires by the thought of unified things such as renunciation ([ps1.1:497.1]()). This emphasizes skill in _samādhi_, whereas for “evolution of perception”, one “turns away” through perception based on the predominance of understanding ([ps1.1:496.1](); see Bodhi’s note on this Sutta for the commentary and subcommentary). This use of “perception” is seen in such texts as [an10.60](), where a series of “ten perceptions” mostly focus on the development of insight, i.e. the “predominance of wisdom”. This explanation matches well with Cūḷapanthaka’s verses, which do indeed emphasis his focus on oneness as leading to immersion. However, Mahāpanthaka’s verses emphasize energy rather than insight.
an1.200:1.1: Mahāpanthaka’s verses are at [thag8.3](), where he tells of undertaking the resolve to not sit down until awakened.
an1.201:1.1: It seems Subhūti’s support of his fellow monk Saddha ([an11.14]()) was why he was foremost in non-strife ([mn139:14.3]()); he was additionally praised as worthy of donations. Subhūti’s meditation is praised at [ud6.7](), and his verse opens the Theragāthā at [thag1.1]().
an1.203:1.1: Revata of the Acacia Wood has some verses at [thag14.1](), with another isolated one at [thag1.42]().
an1.204:1.1: Praised at [ud5.7](), his verse at [thag1.3](), Revata the Doubter’s doubts regarding points of Vinaya were resolved by the Buddha at [pli-tv-kd6:16.1.1]().
an1.205:1.1: According to his verses ([thag13.1]()), Soṇa Koḷivisa was former footman to the king of Aṅga. Raised in luxury, his overexertion in meditation was addressed with the famous simile of the harp ([pli-tv-kd5](), [an6.55]()). | His second name is quite uncertain. The commentary says it is a clan name, proposing the spelling _koṭivessa_, the most powerful of the merchants. The Sanskrit spelling is _koṭīviṃśa_, said to be an epithet due to receiving a gift of “twenty ounces” of gold. Neither of these seem particularly persuasive.
an1.206:1.1: Given the going forth by Mahākaccāna, Soṇa of the Sharp Ears undertook the arduous journey from Avanti to visit the Buddha, where he recited the Chapter of the Eights ([ud5.6](), [pli-tv-kd5:13.9.5]()). His verses are at [thag5.11](). There is no evidence that his pointy ears indicate an elven ancestry.
an1.207:1.1: All we know from the early texts is his verse at [thag1.60](). Later legends vary: he was a Sakyan, or else a prince of Varanasi, or else the baby born of Suppāvāsa in [ud2.8](). His abundance in possessions was ascribed to his generosity in past lives; Sīvali is much revered in Theravada as a patron of prosperity and safety for travelers.
an1.208:1.1: Vakkalī’s faith is referenced at [snp5.19:16.1](), and his verses are at [thag5.8](), but he is best known for his extreme devotion to the Buddha while terminally ill ([sn22.87]()).
